lesson.title: Why Water Bends and Ammonia Isn't Flat
lesson.summary: Lone pairs take up more space around a central atom than bonding pairs do, so the extra repulsion they cause squeezes real bond angles smaller than the idealized VSEPR geometry predicts.
lesson.body:
VSEPR theory starts from a simple idea: every group of electrons around a central atom, whether it is tied up in a bond or sitting alone as a lone pair, repels every other group and pushes to get as far away as possible. That competition for space is what produces the five basic electron domain geometries, from linear all the way to octahedral. But VSEPR gets more precise once you stop treating every electron domain as identical. Lone pairs and bonding pairs do not repel their neighbors with equal force, and that difference changes real, measured bond angles in ways that pure geometry alone would not predict.

The reason comes down to how each type of electron pair is held. A bonding pair is stretched between two nuclei, both of which pull on it, so its electron cloud is relatively thin and elongated along the bond axis. A lone pair belongs to only one nucleus. With nothing pulling from a second atom, it spreads out closer to the central atom and occupies a fatter, more diffuse region of space. A bigger, closer electron cloud pushes harder on its neighbors. That single fact explains the entire hierarchy of repulsion strength chemists use: lone pair to lone pair repulsion is strongest, lone pair to bonding pair repulsion is intermediate, and bonding pair to bonding pair repulsion is weakest.

You can see this hierarchy directly by comparing three molecules that all have four electron domains around the central atom, and therefore the same underlying tetrahedral electron domain geometry, but different numbers of lone pairs. Methane, CH4, has zero lone pairs on carbon, so its four bonding pairs repel each other evenly and the H-C-H angles sit at the ideal tetrahedral value of 109.5 degrees. Ammonia, NH3, has one lone pair on nitrogen. That lone pair pushes the three N-H bonding pairs closer together than 109.5 degrees, compressing the measured H-N-H angle down to about 107 degrees, even though nitrogen is still tetrahedral in its electron domain geometry.

Water pushes the trend further. Oxygen in H2O carries two lone pairs, and two fat, close-in electron clouds crowd the two O-H bonding pairs even more aggressively than ammonia's single lone pair did. The result is a measured H-O-H bond angle of about 104.5 degrees, noticeably tighter than both methane and ammonia, even though water's electron domain geometry is still, at its core, tetrahedral. This progression, 109.5 degrees, then 107 degrees, then 104.5 degrees, is one of the cleanest demonstrations in introductory chemistry that molecular shape and electron domain geometry are not always the same number, and that lone pairs are the reason why.

This distinction matters far beyond memorizing three angles. Whenever you predict a molecular shape, you first count all electron domains to get the underlying geometry, then you subtract out the lone pairs to name the actual molecular shape, and finally you nudge the angles inward wherever a lone pair is doing the crowding. Later, when hybridization gives you a physical picture of the orbitals that hold these bonding and lone pairs, and when dipole moments ask you to add up bond polarities in three dimensions, the compressed angles you learn here are exactly what determines whether those bond dipoles cancel or reinforce each other.
